extracted.intended_audience: artists and students of landscape painting; art critics interested in faithful depiction of skies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for observing and representing skies and clouds in landscape art, with distinctions between cloud regions (cirrus/central/rain-cloud) and detailed prescriptions on form, colour, light, and truthful rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of sunbeams (avoid visionary rays)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is utterly false in principle to represent the visionary beam, and we ought only to show that which has actual existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beams can only appear where there is a cloud or solid body between the observer and the sun; they almost invariably begin on the dark side of clouds, the orb itself remaining the centre of a broad blaze. Do not draw spiky rays issuing from the sun as if originating at the orb (these are effects of the dazzled eye and not real). If representing rays that seem to issue from near the sun, make them broad bursts of light that begin at clouds (Turner's practice), not thin spiky shafts. Examples: Rogers plates and Turner's works—beams begin where clouds do, not traced to the sun. Symbolical or 'visionary' rays suit religious symbolism but are out of place in pure landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent only actual optical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Show only those effects which have actual existence rather than those perceived by the dazzled eye or purely symbolic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to represent rays seen by a dazzled eye you must accept the attendant phenomena (e.g., pink and blue circles). Prefer rendering physical causes and real appearances (cloud-born beams, broad bursts, blazes of united light) rather than optical after-images or symbolic shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect medium-specific capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not directly compare drawings (watercolour) with oil paintings; wash/sponging and other watercolour artifices produce appearances not easily attainable in oils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some delicate effects achieved in watercolour (wash, sponging) give a quality difficult to reproduce in oil; when judging or attempting to imitate, account for differences of medium and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide atmosphere into three cloud regions and depict accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the sky divided into three regions—upper (cirrus), central (stratus/central region), and lower (rain-cloud)—each inhabited by clouds of specific character different from the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each region has its own forms and laws; accurate representation depends on placing clouds at the right altitude and using the appropriate formal, tonal, and colour characteristics for that region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-region (cirrus) — Symmetry and systematic arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper clouds are nearly always arranged in some definite and evident order, commonly in long ranks composed of transverse bars of about the same length, often forming networks or radiating fibres ('mares' tails').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render upper clouds as disciplined systems (long ranks, parallel bars, radiating parallel fibres) oriented with the wind; avoid depicting them as isolated, random puffiness—symmetry and plan are essential features of the cirrus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-region (cirrus) — Sharpness of edge
rubrics_metrics.description: Edges of the cirrus bars turned to the wind are often the sharpest outlines the sky shows; the opposite edges are soft or imperceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture contrast of a razor-sharp windward edge with a melting, soft leeward edge. When both edges are soft (calm conditions) clouds appear round and fleecy; use edge quality to indicate wind and atmospheric conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-region (cirrus) — Multitude (number)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cirrus displays an infinity of division — long ranks severed into countless small undulatory masses; number is felt most when symmetrical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey the impression of vast number (countless lines, divided bars) — the feeling of multitude is an important attribute. Use repetition, systematic division, and textural variation to express this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-region (cirrus) — Purity of colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper clouds are composed of the purest aqueous vapour and receive sunlight through less-dense atmosphere, so their colours are purer, more vivid, and their whites less sullied than lower clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clearer, more vivid hues and cooler grays for dark sides; respect the increased intensity and purity of light at altitude when modelling colour and value in cirri.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper-region (cirrus) — Variety of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Although symmetric as systems, individual cirrus members show marked dissimilarity; nature never lets members of disciplined groups be alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the overall system, give each cloud-element distinct character—different fineness, curvature, number, and modelling—so that variety and unity coexist. Avoid repeating identical cloud-forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study clouds from nature; rapid, accurate sketching
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds change quickly; to know where truth lies you must sketch clouds rapidly and accurately in outline from nature rather than 'daubing down effects' from imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make quick studies on the spot to capture outlines and essential structure; reliance on studio invention leads to falsehood—rapid field sketches preserve the specific character required for fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cirrus to express both transparency and mist by edge and form variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner uses sharp-edged cirri to indicate transparency of air, and fleecy/unified cirri to express mist; sunbeams' edge definition varies with the mistiness of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for transparency, employ sharp windward edges and avoid edged sunbeams near the sun (keep the orb as a blaze). For misty atmospheres, render cirri fleecy and mingling, with sharp sunbeams terminated by definite shadow — adjust cloud-edge treatment to communicate atmospheric quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and coherence of all minor features
rubrics_metrics.description: The best works show 'perpetual consistency in all points'—concentration on every fact, watchfulness of the entire meaning and system of nature so all parts testify to the same truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every small detail (edge treatment, shadowing, reflexes, interval air) aligns with the overall atmospheric logic and enhances verisimilitude; avoid isolated accurate details that contradict the general conditions of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render spatial depth and interpenetration of cloud-planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper clouds should show varying indications of space and depth so one can look through and through from one cloud to another, feeling how they retire to the horizon and melt into recesses of sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graduated tones, translucency, and subtle colour shifts in interstices to depict depth; ensure intervals read as 'absolute air' and not just flat separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour complexity at small scale (upper clouds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The colours of cirri are marvellous in their changefulness—near-zenith colour changes over small areas, with each cloud showing distinct dark-sides, edges and gradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uniform blue fields and identical cloud coloration. Paint small-scale, repeated gradations—fringes of milky white, purple dark-sides, orange undersides, edges of gold—so each square yard contains variety without repeating another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central-region — recognize and depict ragged, clumsy, scattered vapor when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The central region's typical cloud is a white, ragged, irregular, scattered vapor with little form or colour; on canvas this often serves to introduce light and break monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting lower-central skies or Dutch-style scenes, a cautious, lightly glazed treatment may suffice. But be aware these clouds are comparatively uninteresting and may be used as neutral ground rather than as a subject of delicate observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central-region — angular forms and decision of outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds of the central region often display marked angular outlines—steady right lines and grotesque peaks—reflecting temperature boundaries and fixed radiant-heat lines rather than random wind impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict large-scale angular massing and firm outlines where clouds are governed by mountain-induced temperature lines or fixed atmospheric structures; model smaller curvilinear detail within that greater angular framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud formation governed by temperature lines, not merely wind impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds are often rendered locally visible by falls of temperature; outlines are bounded by changes of temperature rather than by wind impulses, so parts may appear, disappear, or remain stationary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing cloud motion or persistence, indicate formation/disappearance of parts rather than simple translational movement. Represent recurrent localized spots of cloud growth (e.g., over mountain flanks) that increase and diminish in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of minor curves — curvilinear but never monotonous
rubrics_metrics.description: The minor contours that make up larger cloud outlines are beautifully curvilinear but not monotonous in their curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive, identical rounded motifs; compose minor curves with varied rhythms and amplitudes so they contribute to a lively, expressive larger outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on 'effects' or facile imitation (old masters' pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many old-master skies are 'toneless, crude, and wanting in depth and transparency' or filled with coarse, common effects chosen for facility rather than observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cover canvas with formulaic daubs of cloud to imitate a master; prefer studied observation and truthful representation. Be suspicious of easy techniques that hide lack of knowledge (e.g., uniform blue fields with similar clouds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism has limited place in pure landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism is often of the highest use in religious art and in some measure allowable in all art, but is out of place in pure landscape where fidelity to observable truth is the aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve symbolic devices (daring black sunbeams, spiky rays) for contexts that justify them (religious, allegorical). In pure landscape pursue descriptive truth rather than symbolic shorthand, though accept limited exceptions with intention and awareness.
